title: Bix's contribution, and Trumbauer
summary: Reel change; Hug calls each Bix solo a masterpiece and Trumbauer underrated; their chase choruses.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: I got the second reel on. Okay. Mr. Huck. Ready to go. Okay. You want to ask a question?

Yeah, well, it's just that is there any value in trying to say that... trying to trace this to Emmett Hardy or what? I mean, it's obvious that Emmett Hardy was probably a great musician. I mean, you know, a lot of people testify to that. And that he probably had an influence on Bix's style. But what did Bix have... what did he contribute to the course of musical development? I guess you could say of jazz since the New Orleans style. Was his influence or contribution musically a harmonic in his use of harmonies? Or... Then I'm going to ask you to play some piano in which you kind of point out what he did, what he seems to have contributed. Yeah, you mean what Bix contributed?

Right. Well, I can only say that as far as I'm concerned, he contributed. He contributed so much that it would be just hard to say what he did contribute, accepting that we know that all of these solos that he played were so original and so meaningful and so beautiful that really, if you analyze each one of his solos, they become almost... They become a masterpiece. Each one of them are a masterpiece. And you can almost make a tune or an arrangement out of each one of his solos. Yeah. Which is so amazing. I mean, you hardly hear anyone who had such original solos as he had. The only ones that come to my mind is like Armstrong and Bonnie Berrigan. You know, a few people that really had solos that really stayed with you. I mean, so that you couldn't forget them. How long since you've heard a Bix record? How long since you've heard one? Well, I haven't played one now. Quite about six months a year, maybe.
Yeah, and you remember every solo. Pretty near. Very few of them. That's the most fantastic thing. And he remembers Trumbau by solos, too.

Trumbau. Frankie Trumbau, to me, I think that he was really great. I mean, to me, he is very, very underrated. Uh-huh. Even to when he was playing with Bix, Bix was so strong, you see, that he overshadowed anyone and everyone. And, of course, I think that really Trumbau did a lot to enhance him when they were playing together. Uh-huh. Because it seemed as though that Trumbau knew every move that he made. Uh-huh. There was nothing that Bix ever did that you wouldn't hear Trumbau right along with him. And it sounds as though you wouldn't know whether Trump, whether Bix got it from Trumbau or Trumbau got it from Bix. Uh-huh. I mean, you really couldn't figure it out. It was so close. Uh-huh. I think it was a beautiful team. Uh-huh. I don't know of any two musicians that complemented each other so well as they did. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Beautiful, beautiful combination. And I think they originated the so-called chase choruses in some of those numbers where back and forth they would answer each other.

Where they would answer one another. Yeah. Oh, definitely. That was beautiful. Yeah. You took advantage of me. And I can't start to think of all of the ones that they did that on. But it was just fantastic.
